source_refs.note: Exercise 2.1, Question 4: Exercise 2.1, book pages 26-27: Q1-Q11 (33 parts)

blocks.prompt: 4 (i) Find the domain and the range of the function \(g\) defined below: \(g(x) = 5 - x\).
blocks.explanation:
Domain: all inputs we may use. Range: all outputs that actually come out.
\(g(x) = 5 - x\) is a straight line with no root and no fraction.
Plan: check what could go wrong for the domain; solve \(y = 5 - x\) for \(x\) for the range.
steps:
Given: \(g(x) = 5 - x\).
To find: domain and range.
Method: Only a square root of a negative number or division by zero can restrict the domain. For the range, check that every \(y\) is reached.

Domain
\[\text{Domain } g = (-\infty, \infty)\]
Why: \(5 - x\) can be worked out for every real \(x\).

Range
\[y = 5 - x \Rightarrow x = 5 - y\]
Why: For any real \(y\), the input \(x = 5 - y\) is real and gives \(g(5 - y) = 5 - (5 - y) = y\). So every real \(y\) is an output.

Check
\[y = 100:\; x = -95,\ g(-95) = 100 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Any chosen output really comes out.

blocks.prompt: 4 (ii) Find the domain and the range of the function \(g\) defined below: \(g(x) = \sqrt{x + 2}\).
blocks.explanation:
A square-root function: the number under the root must not be negative.
We must find the allowed inputs and the outputs.
Plan: solve \(x + 2 \ge 0\); then use "a square root is never negative".
steps:
Given: \(g(x) = \sqrt{x + 2}\).
To find: domain and range.
Method: Domain from \(x + 2 \ge 0\). Range: \(\sqrt{\ }\) gives \(0\) or positive values only.

Domain
\[x + 2 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge -2\]
\[\text{Domain } g = [-2, \infty)\]
Why: The root of a negative number is not real. \(x = -2\) is allowed (\(\sqrt{0} = 0\)), so the bracket is square.

Range
\[g(-2) = 0,\ g(2) = 2,\ g(98) = 10\]
\[\text{Range } g = [0, \infty)\]
Why: The smallest output is \(0\) at \(x = -2\); outputs grow without limit. Any \(y \ge 0\) comes from \(x = y^2 - 2 \ge -2\).

Check
\[y = 3:\; x = 7,\ \sqrt{9} = 3 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A chosen output is really produced, and no negative output is possible.

blocks.prompt: 4 (iii) [printed as (iv); the book skips the label (iii)] Find the domain and the range of the function \(g\) defined below: \(g(x) = \begin{cases} 6x + 7, & x \le -2 \\ 4 - 3x, & x > -2 \end{cases}\).
blocks.explanation:
A piecewise function: one rule for \(x \le -2\), another for \(x > -2\).
We must find the domain and the range.
Plan: find the outputs of each piece on its own interval (watch the endpoint), then take the union.
steps:
Given: \(g(x) = 6x + 7\) for \(x \le -2\); \(g(x) = 4 - 3x\) for \(x > -2\).
To find: domain and range.
Method: Domain: every \(x\) belongs to one piece. Range: union of the outputs of the two pieces.

Domain
\[(-\infty, -2] \cup (-2, \infty) = (-\infty, \infty)\]
Why: Every real number is either \(\le -2\) or \(> -2\), and both rules are lines (no roots, no fractions).

Outputs of piece 1 (\(x \le -2\))
\[g(-2) = 6(-2) + 7 = -5\]
\[\text{outputs } (-\infty, -5]\]
Why: Slope 6 is positive, so the largest output is at the largest allowed \(x = -2\), which is included. Going left, outputs fall without limit.

Outputs of piece 2 (\(x > -2\))
\[4 - 3(-2) = 10 \text{ (not reached)}\]
\[\text{outputs } (-\infty, 10)\]
Why: Slope \(-3\) is negative, so outputs are largest just to the right of \(-2\): close to 10 but never 10, because \(x = -2\) is not in this piece. Going right, outputs fall without limit.

Union of the pieces
\[(-\infty, -5] \cup (-\infty, 10) = (-\infty, 10)\]
Why: \((-\infty, -5]\) lies inside \((-\infty, 10)\). No input gives 10 or more.

Check
\[x = -1.9:\; g = 4 + 5.7 = 9.7\]
\[x = -3:\; g = -18 + 7 = -11\]
Why: Outputs come close to 10 but stay below it; see the graph. An output like 12 would need \(4 - 3x = 12\), \(x = -\frac{8}{3}\), which is not \(> -2\).

answer_figure.alt: Graph of the piecewise function g on axes from x = -4 to 4. For x up to -2 it is the steep rising line y = 6x + 7, ending in a filled dot at (-2, -5). For x greater than -2 it is the falling line y = 4 - 3x, starting at an open circle at (-2, 10) and going down to the right through (0, 4) and crossing the x-axis at 4/3. A dashed horizontal line at y = 10 shows the height that is never reached.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints five answers, (i) to (v), for a question with four printed parts, and its (iv) gives Range \(g = (-\infty, \infty)\) for this piecewise function. That is wrong: no input gives an output of 10 or more. The correct range is \((-\infty, 10)\); the domain \((-\infty, \infty)\) is right.

blocks.prompt: 4 (iv) [printed as (v); the book skips the label (iii)] Find the domain and the range of the function \(g\) defined below: \(g(x) = |x - 5|\).
blocks.explanation:
An absolute-value function: \(|\ |\) gives the size of a number without its sign.
We must find the domain and the range.
Plan: every real number has an absolute value; an absolute value is never negative.
steps:
Given: \(g(x) = |x - 5|\).
To find: domain and range.
Method: Domain: nothing can go wrong. Range: \(|x - 5| \ge 0\), with \(0\) at \(x = 5\).

Domain
\[\text{Domain } g = (-\infty, \infty)\]
Why: \(x - 5\) and its absolute value exist for every real \(x\).

Range
\[g(5) = 0,\ g(8) = 3,\ g(2) = 3\]
\[\text{Range } g = [0, \infty)\]
Why: The smallest output is 0 (at \(x = 5\)). Any \(y \ge 0\) comes from \(x = 5 + y\). Negative outputs are impossible.

Check
\[y = 7:\; x = 12,\ |12 - 5| = 7 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A chosen output is produced; \(g(x) = -1\) has no solution.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key's (v) prints Range \(g = (-\infty, 2) \cup [7, \infty)\) for \(g(x) = |x - 5|\). That is wrong: an absolute value is never negative, and every \(y \ge 0\) is reached. The correct answer is Domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), Range \([0, \infty)\). (The key's extra "(iii)" line, Domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), Range \([0, \infty)\), is in fact this answer.)
